what_its_for: Tesamorelin is used to reduce excess belly fat (called lipodystrophy) in adults with HIV who are taking HIV medicines. It works by mimicking a natural hormone in your body called growth hormone-releasing factor, which helps your body make more growth hormone and reduce fat buildup in the abdomen.
how_to_take: Tesamorelin is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection) in your belly area. Your healthcare provider will show you exactly how to mix and inject this medicine. Always rotate the injection site so you are not injecting in the exact same spot every time. Inject it in the morning on an empty stomach or at least 30 minutes before eating. Never inject into a vein or muscle.
dosing: The usual dose is 2 mg injected under the skin once daily. Your doctor will determine the right dose for you. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next scheduled dose the following morning. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store unmixed (unreconstituted) vials in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Keep the vials in their original box and protect them from light. Once you mix the powder with the sterile water, use it right away or within 3 hours if kept in the refrigerator. Never freeze the mixed solution. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid using tesamorelin if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Do not use it if you have certain types of cancer, or active tumors in your brain or pituitary gland. Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, especially corticosteroids (like prednisone), because tesamorelin may change how they work in your body. Avoid injecting into scars, bruises, or areas with skin irritation.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: unusual swelling or fluid retention in your hands, feet, or ankles; joint pain or muscle aches that are severe; numbness or tingling in your hands or wrists (tunnel syndrome); changes in your blood sugar levels (increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision); injection site reactions like redness, swelling, bruising, or pain that does not go away; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, hives, shortness of breath, or swelling of the face or throat. Also call your doctor if your belly fat does not seem to be improving after a few months of treatment.
when_it_works: Most people start to see a reduction in belly fat after about 26 weeks (6 months) of daily use. Some improvement may be noticed sooner. Keep taking your medicine every day as directed, even if you do not see changes right away. If you stop taking tesamorelin, the belly fat may come back.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use tesamorelin if you are pregnant, as it may harm the unborn baby. Women of childbearing age should use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Breastfeeding: It is not known if tesamorelin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Older adults (65 and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to the side effects of tesamorelin, especially fluid retention and joint pain. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: Tesamorelin is not approved for use in children.
